summary: Silver birch (Betula pendula) is a deciduous tree native to Europe, Morocco, temperate Asia, Canada and Alaska. Its white peeling bark and slender, often drooping twigs make it distinctive, while masses of winged seeds let it colonise bare or fire-swept ground early. Its open canopy admits enough light for shrubs and other plants beneath, and birch woodland supports many insects, birds and animals. The wood, bark and twigs have long supplied timber, fuel, roofing, crafts and brooms.

Rotheca myricoides is an evergreen flowering shrub native to tropical eastern Africa, especially mountain regions extending from Eritrea to South Africa. Its pale blue or mauve flowers have long projecting stamens and styles, giving them a butterfly-like appearance. Long flower tubes suit visitors with long mouthparts, while pollinated plants form small black fruits eaten by birds, which helps spread the seeds. Its leaves are often velvety and release an unpleasant scent when crushed.

Flooded gum (Eucalyptus grandis) is a tall, straight-trunked tree found along coastal and subcoastal eastern Australia. It dominates wet forest and rainforest margins on deep, fertile soils, sometimes forming pure stands. Its smooth pale bark is interrupted by a rough brown skirt around the lower trunk. Fast growth and straight-grained, pinkish timber have made it important for plantations, pulp, flooring, joinery, boat building and plywood well beyond Australia.

Northern catalpa (Catalpa speciosa) is a deciduous tree native to the midwestern United States. It bears large heart-shaped leaves, clusters of white trumpet-shaped flowers marked with yellow and purple, and long capsules that can remain through winter before releasing winged seeds. Farmers planted this fast-growing tree for fence-post timber. It also hosts catalpa moth caterpillars, which may strip its leaves but rarely cause serious harm and are prized as fishing bait.

White campion (Silene latifolia) is a hairy flowering plant native to most of Europe, western Asia and northern Africa. Male and female flowers grow on separate plants, with sex determined by X and Y chromosomes. Its white, deeply notched flowers sit above an inflated calyx and bloom from late spring into early autumn. A specialised fungus, Microbotryum violaceum, spreads between flowers and sterilises infected plants, functioning much like a sexually transmitted infection.

Pachycereus pecten-aboriginum is a tall, branching columnar cactus endemic to Mexico. Its evening-opening white flowers are pollinated by nectar-feeding bats in Tehuacán, while Sonoran flowers remain open longer and also attract daytime visitors. The large fruits split when ripe to expose red pulp and black seeds. Indigenous peoples used the spine-covered fruits as combs, a practice remembered in the scientific name through its reference to native combs.

summary: Tree rhododendron (Rhododendron arboreum) is an evergreen shrub or small tree found from the Himalayas and Tibet through parts of South and Southeast Asia. In early and mid-spring it produces dense clusters of red, pink or white bell-shaped flowers, each marked with dark nectar pouches and spots. Its broad, dark green leaves have a silvery, fawn or brown hairy coating beneath. It is Nepal’s national flower.

Mediterranean saltwort (Caroxylon vermiculatum) is a small perennial shrub native to arid and semi-arid parts of the Middle East, North Africa and southern Europe. Its grey, repeatedly branching stems carry tiny, hairy scale-like leaves and small flowers with pinkish winged sepals. It is an important dry-country fodder plant for cattle, sheep, goats and camels, although overgrazing has made it increasingly rare alongside other useful forage species on the Jordanian steppe.

Hochstetter’s butterfly orchid (Platanthera azorica) is an exceptionally rare Azorean orchid distinguished by flowers larger than those of the archipelago’s other butterfly orchids. Rediscovered in 2011 on a single upland ridge on São Jorge, it was later found flowering on neighbouring Faial in 2017. That rediscovery prompted a reassessment of old specimens and revealed that plants previously grouped together actually represented three distinct species. Genetic evidence traces their lineage to Europe or North Africa.

Calendula suffruticosa is a small, self-supporting herb in the daisy family, with broad leaves and usually yellow or orange flower heads. The species varies greatly across its range and is divided into numerous subspecies, many tied to narrow coastal, island or rocky habitats around the western Mediterranean, North Africa, Madeira and the Canary Islands.

Stinking hellebore (Helleborus foetidus) is an evergreen perennial native to mountainous parts of central and southern Europe and Asia Minor. Its upright stems carry drooping yellow-green flowers, often edged purple, whose numerous nectaries attract bees and other insects. Yeasts living in those nectaries can warm the flowers, possibly helping their scent travel and draw pollinators. The common name is misleading: only the crushed foliage has a notably pungent smell.

Austrocylindropuntia subulata is a branching cactus native to the Peruvian Andes, where it is common above 3,000 metres. Its stems bear spiralling bumps, each tipped with an areole that produces long grey-white spines and awl-shaped rudimentary leaves. Introduced around the Mediterranean as an impassable hedge, it escaped cultivation and became invasive in coastal and some inland Iberian areas; it is also a nationally significant weed in Australia.

Primrose jasmine (Jasminum mesnyi) is a scrambling evergreen shrub native to Vietnam and southern China. Its glossy leaves frame fragrant yellow flowers in spring and summer, with year-round flowering possible in warmer climates. The cultivated form usually has semi-double blooms, and with support the plant can be trained as a slender climber. It is not frost-hardy and needs regular pruning where space is limited; its essential oil is also used in perfumery.

Wood sanicle (Sanicula europaea) is a perennial of shady European woodlands. It has glossy, deeply lobed leaves and tight, rounded clusters of pinkish flowers, followed by bristly fruits that hitch rides on clothing and animal fur. The plant has a long place in European herbal tradition, especially in preparations associated with wound care and cleaning, while its name comes from the Latin sanus, meaning healthy.

Alstroemeria aurea is a flowering perennial native to Chile and Argentina. Brittle, fleshy roots support upright leafy stems crowned in early to midsummer by many orchid-like yellow or orange flowers, often spotted or striped with red or brown. Although widely grown as an ornamental, it can spread rapidly when left undisturbed in favourable conditions. It has also become naturalised in Australia, New Zealand and the United Kingdom.

Echeveria affinis is a Mexican succulent native to the Durango–Sinaloa border and Chihuahua in the Sierra Madre Occidental, with occasional records from San Luis Potosí. It grows at high elevations in very dry, rocky places and is adapted to poor soils rich in mineral material. The species is heavily traded and has produced many horticultural hybrids.

Fumaria reuteri is a flowering plant in the poppy family. The supplied account records it from mainland Portugal and identifies it as native there. It is not protected under Portuguese or European Community legislation according to that account.

Madeiran ivy (Hedera maderensis) is an evergreen climber endemic to Madeira. Common on rocky slopes, soil and tree trunks, especially in laurel forest, it uses aerial rootlets to cling to trees, cliffs and walls and can grow as ground cover when no upright surface is available. Its stems may be tinged red or purple, while mature fruits are round and black. It has also been cultivated for gardens and floral arrangements.

Trifolium diffusum is a flowering clover in the legume family. The supplied account records the species from mainland Portugal and identifies it as native there. It is not protected under Portuguese or European Community legislation according to that account.

Panicled willowherb (Epilobium brachycarpum) is a tall annual native across much of North America, from Canada through the western United States to southwestern and central Mexico. It grows in varied open ground and woodland and has also been introduced into parts of South America. The thin, sometimes two-metre stems carry narrow curved leaves and pale purple or pink flowers whose deeply notched petals can appear doubled, followed by slender capsules.

Woolly lavender (Lavandula lanata) is an evergreen dwarf shrub native to southern Spain. Its leaves are densely covered in striking silver woolly hairs, the feature reflected in the name lanata, while narrow spikes carry deep violet-purple flowers with the familiar lavender scent. Cultivated for its appearance and fragrance, it suits warm, sheltered sites in full sun and is hardy mainly in mild or coastal climates.

Apple rose (Rosa villosa) is a rose species native to central, southern and southeastern Europe, extending into southwestern Russia. Its fruits persist for about 30 days and contain an average of 23 seeds. Measurements in the supplied account describe the fruits as mostly water, while the dry portion is chiefly carbohydrate with a small amount of lipid. The species is closely related to Rosa mollis and is sometimes confused with it.

Eupatorium lindleyanum is a herbaceous perennial native to China, Japan, Korea and Siberia. It grows from a short underground stem, or rhizome, and reaches roughly 30 to 150 centimetres in height. At least two varieties are recognised in the supplied account: the typical variety lindleyanum and var. eglandulosum.

Blechnum appendiculatum is a fern native from the southern United States through Mexico, the Caribbean and Central America to western South America. Known as hammock fern, sinkhole fern and New World midsorus fern, it grows in rocky hammocks and moist forests.
